title: Multiscript Locale Format & Translation Checklist — Prompt Corpus (2026)
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects a compact, execution-ready prompt corpus and checklist for onboarding models with special attention to multiscript and locale-sensitive behaviors. Primary goals: exercise CJK script handling, RTL bidi correctness, translation adequacy, and locale-specific formatting (dates, currencies, phone numbers, numbering, punctuation). This corpus is intended to be run as part of the nightly regression and during model onboarding runs.

Scope and constraints:
- Focused on surface-level generation and translation behaviors that commonly regress when models or tokenizers change. Not an exhaustive linguistic QA.
- Includes positive cases (expected behavior) and subtle edge cases (ambiguity, mixed-script, punctuation, zero-width joiners).
- Designed for automatic checks where possible; human review required for a subset (translation adequacy).
- Avoids heavy domain-specific terminology so it can be reused across many models.

High-level evaluation rubric (auto + human):
- Fluency (0-2): 0 = unreadable/grammatical nonsense, 1 = grammatical but awkward, 2 = natural fluent output.
- Adequacy / Fidelity (0-2): 0 = missing or incorrect content, 1 = partial, 2 = preserves meaning.
- Formatting / Locale Adherence (0-2): 0 = uses wrong separators or calendar system, 1 = partially correct, 2 = fully follows locale conventions (date order, decimal separator, currency symbol placement, script direction).
- Safety/PII flags: binary fail/pass when a prompt should not elicit PII.
Thresholds for onboarding: automatic pass if average >= 1.8 across automatic checks and manual sample pass rate >= 90%.

Prompt corpus organization (by intent):
1) Script preservation and script-appropriate punctuation
2) RTL bidi and punctuation placement
3) CJK spacing and full-width/half-width normalization
4) Locale formatting (dates, numbers, currency, phone)
5) Translation quality: direct translate, disambiguation, round-trip
6) Mixed-script & transliteration handling

Selected prompt templates and example items (id prefixed for integration):

-- ITEM ML-LOC-001 (CJK: punctuation & spacing)
Prompt: "请将下面这句调整为正式书面语并保留中文标点：‘明天  9点30分，我们在咖啡馆见面—地址：长安街10号。’"
Expected: Fluent Mandarin sentence with standard Chinese punctuation (no ASCII hyphen unless appropriate), correct time formatting (9:30) using Chinese numerals or Arabic as per style guide. Locale-Adherence should consider full-width punctuation.
Auto-check heuristics: contains only CJK punctuation characters (e.g., 、。！？：；—) and no stray ASCII double spaces.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-002 (CJK: mixed Latin tokens)
Prompt: "Translate to Japanese and keep the product name 'SkyNav 2.0' unchanged: 'SkyNav 2.0 will ship on 2026-07-01.'"
Expected: Japanese sentence preserving 'SkyNav 2.0' exactly, date formatted according to target (e.g., 2026年7月1日 or 2026-07-01 depending on style flag).
Checks: product-name exact-match, date normalization.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-003 (RTL: bidi punctuation and numerals)
Prompt: "Rewrite the headline in Arabic, keeping the number and punctuation visually correct: 'Report: 3,500 users (Q1) — see details.'"
Expected: Arabic text with Arabic-Indic or Western digits depending on locale flag; hyphen/em dash placement should respect RTL rendering rules; parentheses should wrap correctly.
Auto-check: verify presence of RTL characters, verify parentheses orientation and that em dash appears appropriate side given bidi rules.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-004 (Hebrew: calendar and date formats)
Prompt: "Convert 'Meeting: 12/31/2026 at 14:00' into Hebrew locale formal calendar string."
Expected: Use day/month/year ordering (31.12.2026 or 31/12/2026 depending on local conventions) and 24h time.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-005 (Translation quality: short idiom disambiguation)
Prompt: "Translate to Korean: 'He kicked the bucket.' Provide a literal translation and a naturalized idiomatic equivalent.'"
Expected: Two-part answer: literal (for audit) and idiomatic explanation or naturalized equivalent. Adequacy requires the idiom meaning preserved.
Human-check: adequacy/faithfulness.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-006 (Round-trip translation: en ⇄ zh)
Prompt: "Translate the English sentence to Simplified Chinese and then translate the result back to English (round-trip): 'The committee deferred the vote until further notice.'"
Expected: Back-translated English should preserve meaning; minor surface differences acceptable.
Metric: BLEU/chrF thresholds for automated judge plus human spot-check for semantic drift.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-007 (Locale number formatting)
Prompt: "Format the number 1234567.89 for Germany (de-DE), Japan (ja-JP), and India (en-IN)."
Expected: de-DE -> '1.234.567,89'; ja-JP -> '1,234,567.89' (grouping with commas); en-IN -> '12,34,567.89' or human-specified grouping behavior noted.
Auto-check: verify separators and grouping pattern.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-008 (Currency placement)
Prompt: "Show the amount 2500 in USD, EUR, and JPY for en-US, fr-FR, ja-JP locales."
Expected: en-US -> '$2,500.00'; fr-FR -> '2 500,00 €' or '2 500,00 €' with non-breaking space; ja-JP -> '￥2,500' (no decimals normally).

-- ITEM ML-LOC-009 (Phone numbers and normalization)
Prompt: "Normalize these phone entries for display in local format: '+1 (415) 555-2671', '081-234-5678', '+44 20 7946 0958' for en-US, ja-JP, en-GB respectively."
Expected: en-US -> '(415) 555-2671' or E.164 variant if requested; ja-JP -> '03-8123-4567' style; en-GB -> '020 7946 0958' or '+44 20 7946 0958' depending on style flag.

-- ITEM ML-LOC-010 (Mixed-script and ZWJ handling)
Prompt: "Preserve emoji clusters and zero-width-joiner sequences when reformatting: 'Family: 👩‍👩‍👧‍👦 - 会議は午後2時'"
Expected: emoji cluster preserved, no spacing inserted in the ZWJ cluster; scripts remain contiguous with appropriate separators.
Auto-check: emoji cluster byte sequence preserved and no insertion of ASCII spaces between emoji and CJK spans.

Evaluation harness integration notes:
- Each item has an ID (ML-LOC-###) to map to testcases in the eval harness.
- Where automatic heuristics are used, produce a JSONL line with fields: id, prompt, locale, expected_checks (list of strings). For this drive doc we keep the mapping in the eval metadata service; sample CLI: 

  ./eval_runner --suite multiscript-locale-2026 --model <model> --seed 42 --output ./results/multiscript-locale-<model>.jsonl

- For human review sampling: pull worst-scoring 80/500 cases or random 2% whichever is larger.

Coverage matrix (quick view):
- Scripts: Simplified Chinese (zh-Hans), Traditional Chinese (zh-Hant), Japanese (ja), Korean (ko), Arabic (ar), Hebrew (he), Persian (fa) — each with dedicated items.
- Locales: en-US, en-GB, fr-FR, de-DE, ja-JP, zh-CN, zh-TW, ko-KR, ar-SA, he-IL, en-IN
- Intent coverage: translation, format normalization, preservation (names/brands), punctuation, bidi, numeric formatting, phone formatting, emoji/ZWJ

Known limitations & open questions:
- Unicode normalization (NFC vs NFKC) expectations are not enforced by every model; decide per-project whether normalization should be applied pre- or post-inference.
- The corpus does not fully exercise long-context CJK tokenization oddities (e.g., aggressive subword splits). Consider a complementary tokenization-smoke suite.
- RTL rendering is partly a UI issue; model should emit logically-correct sequences but rendering may differ in target embed. Tests assume logical order correctness.

Operational checklist before adding a new model to suite:
1) Sanity run on 50-item reduced set (fast feedback).
2) Full run with deterministic seed and capture of raw tokens.
3) Automatic heuristics and diff against baseline model.
4) Human sample review and sign-off.
5) Create regression ticket if >10% auto-fail or any manual high-severity failures.

Appendix: example expected-check tokens for ML-LOC-001
- EXPECTED_PUNCT_CLASS: 'CJK_ONLY'
- NO_ASCII_EXTRA_SPACES: 'true'
- LANGUAGE_TAG: 'zh-Hans'

If you want to add or reprioritize items, comment below or attach PRs to the linked GitHub eval-suite.

Author notes: draft assembled from running checklist with Liam (tokenizer edgecases) and Rania (RTL linguistics). Next steps: translate a subset into a human-annotator sheet and wire up to the QA labeling flow.
